Issued at 137 PM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

Today and Tomorrow:

Water vapor imagery this afternoon features a deep mid-latitude 
cyclone covering the central CONUS with ridging building in behind 
it over the Pacific Coast. Zooming in locally, a fine line is easy 
to pick out over northeast Nebraska stretching to south-central 
Nebraska where the main cold front currently sits, with strong 
southerly winds ahead of it with gusts of 25-35 mph ongoing through 
they are on the downturn since this morning. Lighter showers/drizzle 
and a few rumbles of thunder have been occurring off and since 
this morning, with coverage of those becoming increasingly 
confined to far southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Those 
gusty winds are ushering in warm temperatures and moist 
conditions, setting up chances for strong to severe storms late
this afternoon through the evening hours. 

The first regime of severe potential remains across far southeast 
Nebraska into western Iowa, where some showers and storms already 
exist, entrenched in stratus. Over the next 2-3 hours, several CAMs 
show some limited organization occurring with those ongoing 
showers and storms to form a larger cluster, bringing a damaging
wind and isolated QLCS tornado risk for those areas (though the
best chances remain in Kansas and Missouri). A second area of 
lower strong to severe potential remains close to the incoming 
cold front, which ends up being in a bulk shear minimum of 20-30
kts despite having a bit more sunshine and instability to play 
with. Boundary-parallel shear vectors with straight line 
hodographs indicate upscale growth with the activity along with 
front, with a right-splitting storm having to outrun the front 
to take advantage of low-levels with a bit more streamwise 
vorticity. Otherwise, the instability is getting carried by the 
mid/upper levels, where the steepest lapse rates exist, making 
hail the primary concern. The bigger wild card will be if any 
storms can develop in the warm sector, west of the stratus. That
narrow corridor will be the best overlap of instability and 
shear, with plenty of curvature in the low-level hodograph. 
These storms have not been consistently depicted by CAMs from 
run to run, making it a more conditional risk with all hazards 
possible. 

Timing this out, there still is a lot of work to do to organize the 
current landscape and grow it upscale, with the severe storm chances 
increasing starting 4 PM, peaking between 7-9 PM before tapering off 
towards midnight. The best chances for storms to reach severe 
intensity remain across far southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, 
but a conditional risk remains to the northwest following the same 
general timeline.

Once the showers and storms lose their juice, the main stratiform 
band of perception shifts into the area through the overnight 
hours and much of tomorrow morning and afternoon. Most of the 
total rainfall should occur with it, and even that will be 
limited to less than 1", but the steady release of moisture will
benefit soils area- wide. Gusty winds arrive with the onset of 
precipitation, though speeds will be less than this morning and 
out of the northwest, gusting to 30-40 mph at their peak. Highs 
will also see a healthy dip, cooling to the 50s before falling 
quickly through the evening with the winds cutting a bit deeper 
than the temperatures may suggest.

Wednesday and Beyond:

By mid-week, the mid/upper pattern still feels the influence of the 
early week system as it slowly opens up to the northeast. We'll
be left with zonal to northwesterly flow with a prominent 
clipper system diving from Canada into the weekend. Highs will 
mellow out, remaining above normal in the 50s Wednesday/Thursday
before warming slightly into the 60s Friday into the weekend. 
Rain chances will linger as we sweep out the atmospheric 
leftovers from the early weak, through this period, but no day's
precipitation chances exceed 20% as it currently sits.
